Leet
LEET
adjective / noun (Millennial slang)
Clipped from elite. In 1980s bulletin-board culture, "elite" boards granted members access to pirated software and restricted files; insiders wrote the word in a code that swapped letters for look-alike numbers and symbols: 31337 (eleet), 1337 (leet). The cipher, leetspeak, spread through hacker groups such as the Cult of the Dead Cow and into 1990s–2000s online gaming ("l33t skillz," "n00b," "pwn"), where it marked skill and insider status. By the late 2000s it survived mostly as a self-mocking Millennial joke.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Leet means elite: highly skilled, in the know, part of the inner circle, especially in gaming and hacking. Leetspeak is the code (1337, h4x0r, pwn3d) that once kept outsiders out. The Christian observation: the word is a small picture of an old temptation, the pride of secret knowledge. The early Church fought a whole movement built on it, the gnostic boast of an enlightened few with a hidden code. Scripture answers that the knowledge which matters was spoken in the open. Jesus told the high priest, "I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple … and in secret have I said nothing" (Joh 18:20). The gospel is not a password but a proclamation, and God has chosen to hide it from the self-appointed elite: "thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes" (Mat 11:25). Skill is a gift and may be honoured, and Scripture admires the man "diligent in his business" who "shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29). But "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1Co 8:1). A father tells his son: get good at things, really good, and then use the skill to serve rather than to sort people into insiders and noobs. The circle that matters has a door anyone may enter through Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial slang from 1980s hacker code (1337, from elite) for elite skill and insider status; skill may be honoured, but knowledge puffeth up, and the gospel is proclaimed openly, not passworded (1Co 8:1; Joh 18:20).

expand to see more

LEET, adj. / n. (Millennial gamer and hacker slang; 1980s–2000s; written 1337) Elite; highly skilled; belonging to the in-group. "Leet skills." Leetspeak: the cipher substituting numerals and symbols for letters (h4x0r = hacker).

Now chiefly ironic or nostalgic; survives in usernames and as a programmer in-joke (port 31337).

No Webster 1828 entry for the root elite, a French word that entered general English use after Webster’s dictionary.

Decode for parents: watch for groups whose identity depends on a code that keeps others out; Christ’s people speak plainly.

Key Scripture

Joh 18:20 — "Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing."

Mat 11:25 — "At that time Jesus answered and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes."

1Co 8:1 — "Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth."

Pro 22:29 — "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men."

1Co 1:27 — "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;"

Modern Corruption

Leet prizes exclusive skill and secret code; Scripture honours skill but rebukes the pride of hidden knowledge, because the gospel is proclaimed openly and revealed to babes.

expand to see more

The corruption is gnostic in miniature: worth measured by access to a code the crowd cannot read. Leetspeak was built to exclude, and the elite circle defined itself by who was kept out. That is the opposite of the Kingdom, where "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27), and the treasure is hidden not behind skill but behind humility, so that only those willing to become as little children find it.

The redemption honours real excellence without the velvet rope. The craftsman Bezaleel was filled "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding" to build the tabernacle, and his skill served the worship of a whole people. Teach a gifted child to aim at mastery and to put it at the service of others, to explain rather than to gatekeep, and to remember that the greatest knowledge any of us has was given freely: "the entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple" (Psa 119:130).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin eligere (to choose) → French élite → 1980s BBS "elite" → 31337 / 1337 → 1990s–2000s gamer leet, leetspeak.

expand to see more

Latin eligere — to pick out, to choose; French élite — the chosen part

1980s: "elite" bulletin boards with restricted files; the numeric cipher 31337

1990s: hacker groups and gaming adopt leetspeak (1337, h4x0r, n00b, pwn)

Late 2000s: survives as Millennial irony and programmer in-joke

Biblical anchor: in secret have I said nothing (Joh 18:20); knowledge puffeth up (1Co 8:1)

Usage

""Dude, your speedrun was leet.""

"Get good, then teach; knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1Co 8:1)."

"The gospel has no password: in secret have I said nothing (Joh 18:20)."
